news.title: What's new in Accessibility in iOS 27 for Blind and DeafBlind Users
news.summary: Introduction 15 years ago, I produced my first "What's New in iOS Accessibility" article. Every September since, I've been documenting what my testing of the betas has yielded. There are many welcome mainstream changes in this year's iOS 27, such as the upgraded Siri app, new parental controls, a slider to adjust Liquid Glass, further enhanced Apple Intelligence features, and much more. The new Siri has its own app, and coverage of it is beyond the scope of this article other than to mention it's much more versatile and can assist with all kinds of tasks from asking about your personal data to recipes and so on. Lots of individuals will be reviewing these new features. As I've done for many years now, I'm documenting my findings after testing the new version of iOS throughout the summer to discuss accessibility-specific features which impact blind and DeafBlind users. Following what has become a tradition, Apple began discussing enhancements coming to accessibility with its announcement ahead of Global Accessibility Awareness Day. More info about forthcoming features was detailed during the Worldwide Developers Conference Keynote. Devices that will work with iOS 27, according to Apple, are the iPhone SE 2 and later, as well as the iPhone 11 and later. The page linked to above is also a good resource for mainstream changes coming in iOS 27. VoiceOver Though there are fewer changes in iOS 27 than what were found in iOS 26, VoiceOver has gained quite a bit of new functionality. Whether you are a speech user or a braille one, there are a lot of new offerings in this year's release. Pronounce It Together There is now a setting which allows a VoiceOver user to import or share their pronunciation dictionary. This feature could be helpful when, for example, text-to-speech engines do not pronounce things correctly in local dialects. Instead of everyone having to make the changes, one person could compile it and share it with other users in a similar situation. It could also be used as a form of prank. Imagine changing the pronunciation of a friend's name to a friendly insult along with other changes and they later encounter it. These settings can be found under Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Speech> Pronunciations. Selecting 'Import' will bring up the Files function and allow the user to browse to the file they wish to import. Sharing one's own pronunciations brings up the standard Share Sheet, where the file can be sent to any number of places or contacts. Hide Your Cursor For those who may not be aware, the VoiceOver cursor appears as a black rectangular outline surrounding the item that currently has VoiceOver focus. While handy in some situations such as showing a sighted user where VoiceOver focus is set, helping a low vision user who tracks VoiceOver focus, or when demonstrating VoiceOver support to a developer, there are certainly reasons individuals may wish to disable it. This is because it can also serve as a distraction when the VoiceOver cursor itself isn't an important part of the iPhone's purpose. For example, when using the iPhone for face-to-face communication as a DeafBlind user, it can distract the person you are attempting to communicate with from the text you are typing. Some may wish to hide the visual VoiceOver cursor during screen sharing. To adjust this setting, head to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Cursor Visibility, and choose from showing the cursor, hiding it always, or hiding it during screen sharing. Navigating in New Ways with Explore By Touch iOS 27 brings new options to precisely control VoiceOver's reading of text when using Explore by Touch, or, as it's more commonly referred to, 'dragging your finger around the screen'. Options for Text Exploration are now Paragraph, Line, or Sentence. For example, when set to 'Sentence', VoiceOver will only speak the sentence under your finger instead of the entire element as it previously did. Users can adjust this by going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Text Exploration. Note that changes made in Text Exploration only apply to Explore by Touch, and will not impact swiping through content. At least, not this particular setting. It's for Swipers Too A separate setting, called Text Navigation, offers the ability to modify how VoiceOver moves when swiping left and right through the screen with one finger. The available options are Line, Sentence, Paragraph, and Element. In addition to allowing one to more easily read blocks of text that VoiceOver sees as one large element, having these two new sets of options can give VoiceOver users other choices than the rotor for text navigation. To check out the new settings for swiping, head to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Text Navigation. Remember that you will need to adjust settings for Text Exploration and Text Navigation separately. Hints Become Customizable For a lot of the clients I work with who use speech, the hints offered by VoiceOver can be helpful, but there comes a point where they cause interference with touchscreen navigation once a user advances in their journey of learning VoiceOver. For example, "Double Tap to Open" can grind on one's nerves after a while. When I first started learning to use an iPhone with iOS 4, this was also something I became frustrated with. If the system hints become a nuisance, the user now has more control over them. iOS 27 brings the ability to adjust the amount of delay between when VoiceOver provides active information about what is in focus and when the hint will be conveyed. To configure this, head to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Verbosity> Hints, and then either type the duration in seconds ranging from 0.05 to 2.0, or use the 'Decrement' and 'Increment' buttons. The default is 0.8 seconds. It's also now possible to specify if users want all hints, app-specific hints, or no hints at all. You can find these options on the same screen. No Modifier Required for These Functions For VoiceOver commands to be assigned to keyboard shortcuts, Bluetooth keyboard users have always had to include their chosen VoiceOver modifier along with the command. This is no longer necessary with the function keys located in the top row of many Bluetooth keyboards. The setting must be enabled, which one can do by going to Settings>Accessibility>VoiceOver>Commands and setting the Switch Button for "No Modifier Keys" to on. Instead of having to press, for example, VoiceOver Modifier f8 to launch the VoiceOver Settings menu, users can now simply press F8. Live and Open for Questions Live Recognition was first integrated into VoiceOver with iOS 18. iOS 27, coupled with Apple Intelligence, gives Live Recognition even more power. Activating the 'Ask' button will allow the user to ask about what is currently in the camera's view. It's also possible to tell Live Recognition to focus on a specific thing in your environment. As long as that item is able to be tracked, its actions and movements will often be reported by VoiceOver. Ask is a feature that is highly customizable. Going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Live Recognition allows the user to set up some other options. One can change the default question asked when the button is activated, make the default input either dictation or typing, and have the Volume buttons take a still photo for a follow-up or more detailed description. Ask can be set up with a gesture, Bluetooth keyboard command, the Accessibility Shortcut, or a Perkins-style keyboard command. If none of those are what the user wants, there is also the ability to launch the Ask feature using the Action Button. It can be enabled by going to Settings> Action Button, selecting the Accessibility category, and then choosing 'Ask a Question'. The View From iOS In my view, pardon the pun, the largest upgrade for VoiceOver and braille users in iOS 27 is the massive overhaul of the Image Recognition feature. This is thanks to Apple Intelligence, but I'm sure those using iPhone 15 and earlier devices aren't feeling very thankful, since they do not have access to these features. Unlike the multi-step processes involved with using third-party services for detailed descriptions, Image Recognition descriptions typically take less than three seconds. They can be generated on virtually all images the iPhone encounters, and the user does not need to download or upload each image they wish to have described. It is also possible to describe the screen of the device itself, to ask questions about the image in focus, and to generate a description with the ability to ask a follow-up question immediately. These features can be activated through the VoiceOver rotor or by adding specific functions to gestures. The two devices I have upgraded at this point had the Image Recognition options in the Rotor. If, by chance, your Rotor does not have the Image Recognition option after upgrading, it can be added by going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Rotor> Rotor Items and selecting Image Recognition. Since there are up to seven different options for Image Recognition, Apple has also given users the ability to add and remove what they wish to this rotor item. It can be configured by going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Rotor> Image Recognition Rotor. Each of the available options will be discussed below. Image/Item Description will allow the user to get a description of the image or item that VoiceOver focus is set to. Based on my testing, it is generated in less than three seconds. It will be delivered in the form of a VoiceOver announcement. For those using braille, one can read the description at their own pace by pressing Space with N. When done, pressing space with n will return the user to where they were before. I find this particular function to be wonderful for generating descriptions of things in my Facebook feed, my growing photo library, album art in the Music app, and when reading photo-heavy articles on various news sources. Interestingly, this function is the only one that can be mapped to a Perkins-style keyboard. The other options discussed below are not available for users of Perkins-style keyboards. Using the Copied Speech Rotor option launched with iOS 26, users can copy the description to wherever they want on their iOS device. A simpler solution in some situations is available as discussed below. Ask About Image/Item is another option, which does exactly what the choice says. After selecting this, users are presented with a text field which allows them to type a question. Pressing return or enter will generate a response. The nice thing is that you do not need to generate a general description before asking a question. Placing VoiceOver focus on the image is all that is required. With many third-party applications, one must first wait through getting the general description before they can ask a question. I have solved simple CAPTCHAs by asking my iPhone to provide me with only the text in the image. I can then copy it and solve CAPTCHAs. I have not tried more complex puzzles. Explore Image/Item allows you to get the same description as you get when generating an Intelligent Description, but it is static text instead of a VoiceOver announcement. After the text description, there is an option to ask a question either by typing or voice. Also, when focus is on the description, one can flick up with one finger, or use whatever alternative method, to copy the description. Ask About Screen allows the user to get a description of the screen on their iOS device. It functions the same as the Ask About Image/Item choice, but covers the entire screen. I've found this feature handy for understanding what buttons without labels in applications do. This is far more preferable to activating the button to see what happens. The other two options are Describe Screen and Explore Screen. These work the same as the others documented above, only this applies to your entire screen instead of one item. I mentioned browsing photos above, and when in the Photos app, there is yet another rotor option available called Save Intelligent Image Description. When selected, this will add the description generated to the photo itself which will then be available later. A final setting is the ability to show a list of the recognition options discussed above. It does not have a touch screen gesture assigned to it, but the user can create one. On a Bluetooth keyboard, pressing VoiceOver Modifier, Shift, and R will bring up this menu. Sorry, braille display users, there appears to be no Perkins-style keyboard option. Automatic Image Descriptions Users can head to Settings>Accessibility>VoiceOver>VoiceOver Recognition>Image Descriptions to configure whether image descriptions are provided automatically. One can configure whether they want automatic image descriptions or whether they are conveyed as a fallback when images have alt text. Note that this setting applies to the classic image descriptions, but one will not receive a detailed description such as the ones provided by Apple Intelligence. Braille There are some changes to braille outlined below. As a general usage note, writing longer passages of text seems to be a bit more reliable than it was in all of the iOS 26 releases. Further, there were some issues in iOS 26 with cursor routing buttons not routing correctly and focus jumping back to the top in longer blocks of text while the user was reading. Based on my use, all of these issues have been improved significantly. Predict More Predictably with Braille Screen Input Braille Screen Input now uses the same Predictive Text gestures as the default onscreen keyboard. When typing on the standard touchscreen keyboard, iOS uses Autocorrect and Predictive Text to identify the word you probably intended based on the letters entered, nearby keys, sentence context, and commonly-used language. Braille Screen Input now uses this same prediction system: after entering a word, users can swipe up or down with one finger to move through suggested words or corrections, then continue typing once the desired suggestion is selected. Further, it is now possible to type part of an emoji name and swipe up or down with one finger to find it. Functionality of the BSI Autocorrect requires the primary software keyboard Autocorrect setting to be enabled in Settings> General> Keyboards. Finally, iOS 27 adds the ability to more easily insert alternative characters. To activate alternative character selection, hold the dots of the character you wish to insert until you hear a sound, then release and swipe up or down with one finger to select the desired symbol. A More Flexible Cursor Shifting to braille display users, there is a new setting called 'Snap To Print Text Cursor', which can be found by going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Braille> Cursor Routing. The options are the new Snap To Text Cursor or Any Braille Cell. By default, Snap To Print Text Cursor was selected when I upgraded. The 'Snap to Print Text' setting places the cursor on the closest print text equivalent even when contracted braille is enabled. This setting is particularly helpful for those braille display users using QWERTY keyboards to type while also using contracted braille for reading, as it removes some ambiguity from where the cursor is located. Text Field Labels That Stick Prior to iOS 27, when activating a text field, the text label would disappear entirely. In iOS 27, the label persists even when the text field is active. The label itself appears between two indicator symbols which clearly distinguish the label from the text entered. It can be configured by going to Settings> Accessibility> VoiceOver> Braille> Text Field Labels. The options are to show an abbreviated version of the label or the full thing. Selecting 'Collapse' will provide two indicators without the text label. Selecting 'Full' will display the entire text field label. You can collapse the label by pressing a cursor routing button. If you disable everything in this menu, the behavior will be as it always was in past versions of iOS. Braille Access Expands File Support Braille Access now supports plain text and PDF files. As such, the formerly named 'BRF Files' is now simply called 'Files'. To import these file types, users can follow the same procedures they already use to get BRF content imported. Files are still stored in the 'BRF files' folder on iCloud, so any method a user would utilize to copy text and PDF content is the same. I found that opening plain text files worked quickly, and it was nice to have them imported. Unlike many applications for braille readers, Braille Access tends to remember the place I was in a file when I open it again. PDF content will display, but seems to depend on how well the creator of the file treated accessibility. Formatting such as headings is not preserved. There also appears to be a file size limit, as I was not able to load a PDF file that was 15 MB due to the images it contained. New Features Bring New Keyboard Shortcuts Apple has added a few new options for Perkins-style keyboard shortcuts that people may take advantage of. Under the VoiceOver category, one has been added for launching the Ask function found in VoiceOver Recognition, while another was added for generating an Intelligent Description with Image Recognition. There are no new commands for the other Image Recognition options discussed above. Another mapping option was made available for ignoring trackpads. Hearing On-demand Sign Language Interpreters on FaceTime As part of Apple's Global Accessibility Awareness Day announcement in May, the company shared preliminary details of an API that providers of sign language interpretation apps could use to allow callers to add an interpreter to their FaceTime call. As of the time of writing, there do not appear to be any announcements concerning providers utilizing this API, but hopefully that will come soon. Auto-Caption This Video Captioning automatically produces synchronized subtitles from spoken audio when a video has no existing captions. Apple says it works with videos recorded on the iPhone, videos sent to the user, streamed videos, and other uncaptioned videos played through supported system playback interfaces. When I enabled captioning in the Photos app while playing a video, there were several visual options available for adjusting the output. However, I was not able to find the generated captions with braille. Thankfully, Live Captions under Braille Access works well. Conclusion iOS 27 may not bring as many accessibility changes as its predecessor, but several of its additions are substantial. The expanded image-recognition tools can give blind users faster and more independent access to photos, unfamiliar controls, and other visual information, while the new navigation and customization options allow VoiceOver users to better tailor the experience to their needs. Braille users also gain welcome improvements, including more reliable text editing, clearer text-field labels, and support for additional file formats in Braille Access. Some of the most significant new features require Apple Intelligence, leaving users of older compatible devices without access to everything discussed in this article. There are also a few places where braille keyboard support remains incomplete. Even with those limitations, iOS 27 offers a useful collection of accessibility improvements. As always, individual experiences will vary, and readers are encouraged to share their own observations and bugs in the comments. I also encourage users to check out the AppleVis list of bugs and fixes. If needed, more information on how to update the software on your device is available on this Apple Support page. T

news.title: Final Fortress
news.summary: Final Fortress is a match-3 puzzle. The whole game is the screen of an old terminal: green text, one cursor, and you, the commandant of the last fortress. It is a quiet game. A working console in the dark, the hum of the systems, static like rain. A watch takes fifteen or twenty minutes: do the day's tasks, read what came in, hand over. Nothing hurries you, and nothing happens while you are away. Come back after a week and the fortress is exactly as you left it. Match tiles to finish the day's tasks. Each task brings supplies. Spend them to repair the fortress: reactor, hydroponics, antenna, armory, infirmary. Every repaired system opens new missions. Match 4 or more to charge special tiles. They clear a line, a block, or every tile of one kind. Swap two charged tiles together and they fire as one bigger shape, up to the whole board. The board gets busier as you go: convoy crates that pay out at the bottom, sealed containers with a special tile inside, interference to clear layer by layer, burned sectors the tiles fall past. Some tasks ask for a pattern: decode a sequence in order, or fill a gauge in every column. AI Madness is a mode of its own, outside the fortress. Each shift bends the rules: boards up to 10 by 13, sometimes only three kinds of tile, cascades that barely stop, tasks that may be impossible. On an iPhone with Apple Intelligence, Apple's on-device model (Foundation Models) picks the shift's character and writes its line in the log. Nothing leaves the phone. Otherwise the terminal does the same on its own. Nothing is at stake and nothing is banked. Every shift has a code. Send it to a friend and they get exactly the same board. There is a story in the log: three acts, four threads, and the notes of the commandants who held the fortress before you. It comes a few lines at a time. Read it or skip it. The game never nags about it. Repair the antenna and you will see a board with other players' stations. It is view-only, there is no chat, and it updates once a day. When the story is over, the log keeps going quietly on its own. The music belongs to your fortress alone. The sound is synthesized live and seeded from your fortress, so your station hums like no other and never loops. The hum changes with what is running, with the hour of the night and with the weather outside. Each kind of tile has its own note, and a cascade climbs the scale. One extra room, The Long Dark, carries a call of its own. Three more stations use the instruments in your phone: a weather post that reads the barometer, an acoustic modem and a direction finder. A home screen widget shows your fortress at a glance, in StandBy too. No ads. No lives, timers, energy or streaks. No pop-ups, no push notifications, no accounts, no daily rewards to come back for. Run out of moves and the terminal just says the packet was lost. Try again, nothing is taken away. You can drop a task at any time. Purchases are cosmetic only: screen colors, one extra soundtrack, custom names. Nothing you can buy helps you play, and no purchase moves you up the board. Works offline, on iPhone and iPad. Fully playable with VoiceOver, with a flicker-free stable phosphor mode and a calm mode that softens the board's flashes and haptics.

news.title: Surprise and Shine: Recapping Apple's September 9 Announcements
news.summary: Intro Apple has just wrapped up Surprise and Shine, the big fall announcement event. We got new iPhones, Apple Watches, and (non-pro) AirPods. And yes, the rumors were finally true: one of the new iPhones is a folding one. AirPods have some new tricks, the new Apple Watch has some very nice improvements, and even the normal iPhones are worth checking out. Let's get into it. iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo All of the iPhones announced today share a few features, so we'll start there. At the heart of each new iPhone is the A20 Pro, a system on a chip (SoC) that's better than anything Apple has ever made. So said the presenters, anyway. This is Apple's first 2NM chip, which basically means they shrank the parts so they can fit more into the same amount of space, all while using less power and producing less heat. The A20 Pro comes with four efficiency cores and two cores meant to do serious work, which is the same distribution as last year (six cores, with four efficiency and two powerful ones). The big change here is that the two workhorse cores, called super cores, are beefed up considerably. Apple claims they have desktop performance. The graphics chip has also been upgraded, with seven cores and faster access to the phone's RAM; Apple says graphics run up to 40% faster than the A19 Pro. It's 2026, so we can't not talk about AI, specifically large language models. The A20 Pro has neural accelerators to boost AI performance for the CPU and GPU cores, but the star of the show is the neural engine. Or rather, the engines, plural. Each A20 Pro has two of them, not just one, giving the chip 32 neural cores to work with. Combined with the A20's increased access to memory, Apple said that this is the best chip for mobile AI tasks. All of this performance is going to produce a lot of heat, so Apple took the vapor chamber from iPhone 17 Pro and made some improvements. The way the chip's components transfer heat to the chamber is more efficient now, the materials have been updated, and the design has been altered. The new design has three times the space and is made from a combination of titanium and a special copper alloy. It transfers 40% more heat than the system on iPhone 17 Pro, letting the phone do more work for longer before it has to slow itself down to keep from overheating. Remember Siri AI, a version of Siri that is aware of your locations, messages, and other details? It was announced back in June. If you don't follow Apple news as obsessively as I do, the short version is that Siri is far more aware and capable than before. You can ask for "that recipe Jake sent me a couple months ago", you can issue more natural commands, and you can get much more accurate results with dictation. All of this is kept in a new Siri app, so you can check on past conversations. Oh, and Siri's voice is better than ever. Anyway, Siri AI is fully supported by all the new phones, and Apple spent some time reminding us of what all is going to be possible. There are some extra goodies for Apple Watch Series 12 owners who have Siri AI devices, too, but we'll get to those later. iPhone 18 Pro As has become customary, Apple is offering this year's pro phones in standard and Max variants. The Max has the most battery life of any iPhone ever, while the smaller phone has battery life equivalent to what iPhone 17 Pro Max offers. This seems to be the main difference; both have the same chip, camera, design, and everything else, so I'll just talk about iPhone 18 Pro from here on out. Everything also applies to iPhone 18 Pro Max unless I say otherwise. The stand-out feature of the camera system this year is variable aperture. Specially-designed, tiny pieces in the camera can move to let in more or less light, which also changes the field depth. The aperture widens in low light, closes some in bright light, and can be manually adjusted to change the feel of a picture. I guess professional photographers will be jumping for joy. The A20 Pro's AI capabilities also allow Apple to add more camera enhancements, some of which we knew about already from the iOS 27 announcement at WWDC back in June. What is unique to iPhone 18 Pro, though, is a new set of manual camera controls, called pro controls. These let you change the aperture, white balance, and other settings whose purpose I can only guess at. You can even use AI to keep video locked on a subject. But you're not here for camera details, so let's get on with it. There are a few other, smaller changes compared to iPhone 17 Pro. The new phone can charge faster when plugged in (as opposed to using wireless charging). The Dynamic Island is also smaller and now supports up to three live activities at once. Surprisingly, that's about it. The battery life improvements are great, the A20 Pro sounds like an impressive chip, and the colors have changed (silver, black, glacier, and burgundy). Aside from that, faster wired charging, and the camera improvements, everything seems to be the same. Apple didn't mention the screen, body material, any new or changed buttons, speakers, wifi performance, or anything else. It seems iPhone 18 Pro is, physically, the same as iPhone 17 Pro, just with a new chip and camera. You can pre-order iPhone 18 Pro starting September 12, and it will start shipping on September 18. The Pro starts at $1,199, $1,299 for the Pro Max. This gives you 256GB of storage, just like last year. You can upgrade all the way up to 2TB of storage, the first time any iPhone has offered such a large internal drive. Just know that it won't be cheap. You can also check out the new array of colors for Apple's official cases, cross-body straps, and (new this year) wrist straps. iPhone Duo Apple's first entry into the world of foldable phones is called iPhone Duo . It has a 5.4-inch outer display and unfolds to show a 7.6-inch screen. Both screens have full Apple Pencil support, and the outer screen has Ceramic Shield 2. The frame is high-grade titanium, colored either white or night sky. The side button acts how you expect, but also sports a Touch ID sensor--the phone lacks Face ID. You can add multiple fingers, so that no matter how you happen to hold the phone, the finger resting on the button can unlock it. You can also unlock your phone with your watch. Also, despite being foldable, iPhone Duo has an IP68 rating. That means dust and water will have a hard time getting into it, but you shouldn't take it swimming. Each half of iPhone Duo is very, very thin--after all, the whole package has to be comfortably thin when folded. Apple says that each half is the thinnest iPhone ever produced, which suggests that the halves are thinner than an iPhone Air. Despite this, iPhone Duo has good battery life (30 hours of video playback on the internal screen, 44 when using the outer one) and supports fast wired charging. It also, as mentioned earlier, has the same A20 Pro chip and vapor chamber cooling as iPhone 18 Pro. It even has Apple's custom cellular modem, the C2, giving it millimeter wave 5G support (U.S. only for now) and faster and more efficient cellular communications overall. The camera situation is interesting. iPhone Duo sports the same camera system as iPhone 18 Pro, though without the variable aperture feature. When unfolded, an under-screen selfie camera is available, while a more capable camera lives just above the outer screen. This enables some neat options, such as letting both the photographer and the subject see the camera feed (one person on the inner screen, the other on the outer one) before a picture is taken. If you are taking pictures of children, iOS lets you enable animations designed to draw attention and get the kids' eyes looking toward the lens. When making FaceTime calls, someone can use the inner camera and screen, while someone else can use the outer set, letting two people use the same phone but with different camera feeds. Thanks to its design, you can fold iPhone Duo in such a way that the camera stays pointed where you want without being held. You can let iOS monitor the feed, and take the picture when it thinks you're ready. As to the screen, Apple spent a lot of time talking up the engineering that went into minimizing the crease, getting the under-finger feel right, and more. A special coating makes the screen feel closer to glass than the plasticky feel some folding phones have, while also cutting glare and reflections. Nano-scale layers of lenses help the screen stay bright and readable, while reducing the wear of all the folding and unfolding it will undergo during its life. That's not all the engineering that went into iPhone Duo, either. The frame is not only made of titanium, but reinforced at key points with custom materials for added strength. The hinge is weighted, balanced, and carefully structured to fully support the screen at every point of the folding process. You can set the two halves at any angle (up to 180 degrees) and they will stay there. Use it like a small iPad, set one screen at an angle like a laptop while you type on the other one, or make a tent shape, using the phone like a stand while you watch the outer display. The phone will react how you expect, even going so far as to constantly balance the audio coming from its dual speakers based on how the two halves are configured. iOS 27 has been designed to take full advantage of this phone's unique abilities. You can do a lot of the multi-tasking tricks that you can on iPad, such as opening two apps side by side, quickly moving between on-screen apps, showing a list of emails and an open message at once, and more. You can see two home screen pages at once, and your dock is now vertical. Video controls now appear on the side of the screen, rather than the bottom, so videos have more space and so your thumb can reach the controls. The status bar is smaller and now stays in a corner, again, to give apps more room. Apps have new APIs available, letting them, for example, show a list of options on one half of the screen and a preview of the selected option on the other half. iOS will even detect how the phone is being used and move content toward the edge, so it is easier to tap or see. I realize that much of this section has been about cameras, on-screen layouts, and other things that a lot of you reading this won't care about. That's because that was the focus of the presentation. For now, iPhone Duo feels like a device that will be amazing for plenty of sighted users, but will have less appeal to those of us who use VoiceOver. Low vision folks may love the larger screen, but not being such a person myself, I can't really comment on that. Personally, I'm going to see how things go with this phone, play with one in person once my local stores have some, and not worry about getting my own just yet. I don't know if there will be enough advantage for VoiceOver to justify the cost. Of course, it would be nice to have Touch ID again. iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 for the 256GB model. As with iPhone 18 Pro, you can increase this all the way to 2TB. Preorders open on October 16, with deliveries and in-store availability starting on October 23. AirPods 5 Today brought us a new AirPods model: AirPods 5 . Like the previous generation, they come in two variants, one more expensive than the other. With AirPods 4, the cheaper model lacked active noise cancelation and wireless charging. That's not the case anymore With this new generation, both variants have ANC. The more expensive AirPods add volume adjustment on the stem, just like AirPods Pro, and a case that supports wireless charging. As we've come to expect, the case can handle MagSafe, Qi, and Apple Watch chargers. The premium version also have a five-hour battery life, which is an hour more than what the less expensive ones offer. This is measured with ANC enabled. Both versions of AirPods 5 are, Apple claims, designed to feel and sound better while lasting longer. ANC is 50% more effective than AirPods 4, while transparency sounds more natural. Audio sounds more detailed and rich, and the earbuds can shrug off more sweat and rain than before. They will also work better in even more ear shapes--so Apple says, anyway. No, they are still not available in any color other than white. The less expensive AirPods cost $129, which is what the non-noise-canceling AirPods 4 cost, and this generation includes ANC. That's a good deal, but for just $20 more, you can get on-stem volume controls and a case that can charge wirelessly. That's $149, which is $30 less expensive than the high-end AirPods 4. Apple isn't known for lowering prices, so this is a very pleasant surprise. You can pre-order starting today (September 9). Deliveries will begin arriving September 18, which is also when stores will start offering the new AirPods. Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 The Apple Watch got some nice enhancements this time around. They all apply equally to the Series 12 and Ultra 4, so I will just talk about the new features here. Everything is true of both models, neither of which seems to have changed, physically, from its predecessor. The first improvement is to the heart sensors. Apple Watch has always used lights to measure your pulse, and that hasn't changed. The LEDs in these new models are different, though. Skin contact is better, the LEDs have been arranged in a ring pattern, and the color of the light has gone from red to green. Add in the new electrical sensors for ECG readings, and Apple Watch has never had a more accurate measure of your heart rate. Almost more exciting is how often Apple Watch now takes heart measurements: every five seconds. This is up to sixty times more often than previous Apple Watches did. Heart rate variability (HRV) is now measured every five minutes, which is a 24 times increase. HRV is an indicator of stress and cardiovascular health, so the more (and more accurate) the readings, the better. This generation of watch has better step length tracking as well, meaning that indoor walks and runs will be measured more accurately than before. Apple also claims that this makes Apple Watch the most accurate step tracker of all the modern wearables. They are therefore adding a step count complication, at long last. What will watchOS do with all this data? Apart from your heart rate complication actually showing your current pulse, Apple has made a series of health data improvements. A readiness score suggests whether you should make today a recovery-focused day or a day during which you can push more. On iPhone, your heart and activity data feed a new Longevity feature. You can see how you are doing over time, how your metrics compare to the average person at your age, and what you could do to improve things. To make this feature more accurate, you can take VO2 max, flexibility, movement, and other tests, all done using your iPhone's cameras and live coaching from the app. You can also purchase bloodwork from Quest for $119, directly through the Health app (U.S. only, for now). The results will inform your health insights and recommendations. You can also connect your existing health records, as has been possible for some time. It's not all about health, though. Audio Intelligence is a set of features centered around the microphones in the watch and Siri AI's increased abilities. All of these features are opt-in, meaning they are not enabled by default. Sound Recognition has been on iPhones for years, but now comes to Apple Watch. People who are deaf or hard of hearing can be alerted to sirens, alarms, doorbells, and other sounds. This works even without iPhone nearby. Live Rewind: double press the digital crown and you get a transcript of the last fifteen seconds of conversation. You can read it, or choose to send it to Siri for further use. During the presentation, they showed a server listing food options, then an Apple Watch user bringing up the list as a transcript. It's not clear if you have to activate this feature each time you want the watch to start paying attention, or if it is always available. Siri Recap is a feature you turn on when you want it, such as during a business meeting or an important conversation. Once the event is over, you turn Recap off again. Siri will generate a title and key points from what it heard, letting you review what was said and jog your memory. I assume this also adds to Siri AI's context, letting you ask questions about what was said in the meeting last week, for instance. Shazam for song detection is nothing new, but it is now automatic (once you turn the feature on). You can always know what song is playing near you, without having to ask Siri to do anything. Apple promised that all of these features run locally or, when they don't, are end-to-end encrypted and have extra security built in. No speakers are ever identified or tagged, no audio is saved, nothing is used for training AI. In fact, audio processed by Apple Watch can't leave the system because of how the S11 SoC is designed. Apple has a whole privacy paper about Audio Intelligence if you want to read more. Speaking of the S11 system, let's go over what we know, which isn't much. We know it has something called an Audio Exclave, which is where audio from the watch's microphones is saved and processed. Audio can't leave this isolated part of the system, which is part of how Apple guarantees that Audio Intelligence puts privacy first. The S11 also supports the greatly increased health sensor readings without impacting battery life. Beyond that, Apple made no claims about speed increases, wireless changes or anything else. In a bit of a surprise move, Apple has kept prices the same. The Series 12 starts as $399 for the aluminum casing, while the Ultra starts at $799. Preorders are open today (September 9) and, as with most of what we've talked about here, deliveries and in-store availability start on September 18. The new colors and materials are: aluminum, now with Ceramic Shield 2 glass: black, space gray, light gold, and dark bronze ceramic: pearl white and night blue titanium (Series 12): radiant gold and natural titanium (Apple Watch Ultra 4): black and natural That's All For Now Rumors continue to swirl that Apple has more to show us, so there might be press releases or another event later this year. For now, though, we've covered all the new shinies--iPhone 18 Pro, iPhone Duo, Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5. Plus, version 27 of all of Apple's operating systems comes out on September 14, at which time we will finally get a look at this much-improved Siri that all these new devices were built to support. What caught your metaphorical eye, if anything? Personally, I pre-ordered a Series 12 before I was halfway done writing this article. It'll be a big upgrade over my SE 3, and since most of what I use my Apple Watch for is health-related, I want all the data I can get. I might see about AirPods 5 if a good sale comes along, but I'll wait for the reviews. I like the idea of a folding phone, and I definitely want to play with one in person, but I have no desire to own one. I'm also not planning to get an iPhone 18 Pro, though if Siri AI and upcoming Apple Intelligence features turn out to be as amazing as Apple insists they are, well, we'll see. What do you think? Discuss your excitement, bitter disappointment, or indifference in the comments!

news.title: ghostWriter Markdown
news.summary: Accessibility-first Markdown writing with VoiceOver-friendly editing, document organization, and flexible exports to Word, PDF, HTML, braille, and more. ghostWriter Markdown is a plain-text writing app for notes, articles, lists, documentation, and anything else you want to say with words. It was built accessibility-first. Not accessibility-eventually, or accessibility-in-the-settings-somewhere. VoiceOver was at the center of the design from the first line of code, as the app has been fully created by a Blind developer. If you write with a screen reader, this app was made for you. If you don't, you get a clean, fast, native editor that never gets in your way. So what's Markdown? Markdown adds structure to writing using a few ordinary punctuation marks. A number sign makes a heading. A dash makes a list item. Your document stays readable as plain text, and you can render it whenever you want to see the finished formatting. You don't have to know any of this to start. The Insert feature can add common elements for you, and a built-in Markdown Reference is always a tap away. Writing Made Easy: • A native editor with the Markdown punctuation kept visible, so you always control the source • Insert Actions for links, images, headings, quotes, code, lists, tasks, tables, and rules • Automatic list continuation for bullets, numbers, and task lists • Indent and outdent with tabs or spaces, your choice • Find and Replace, dictation, braille input, and text selection through native iOS controls • A configurable Status Bar showing line, column, word count, current heading, and selection • Automatic saving as you pause, plus Save Now whenever you want it Useful Navigation: • Outline lists every heading in your document and jumps straight to one, moving both the cursor and VoiceOver focus • A 3-finger horizontal swipe with VoiceOver will move the cursor through your document headings while editing • Jump to Line for long documents • Search across document names and their contents • Your last editing position is remembered in every file Keep Files Organized: • Nested folders you can create, rename, move, and navigate • Pin the documents you keep coming back to • Sort by name, created, modified, or last opened • Recently Deleted holds removed files until you restore them or clear them out • Import Markdown, .txt, Word .docx or Powerpoint presentations to convert them into Markdown Render and Share: • See your Markdown as structured HTML right inside the app • Share complete standalone HTML, Markdown, plain text, ePub, tagged PDF, eBraille, BRF, Microsoft Word documents or even Powerpoint presentations • Rendered output uses real semantic headings, lists, tables, links, and landmarks — so what you share is accessible to whoever receives it Your Files, Your Devices: • Documents are ordinary Markdown files, visible in the Files app • Store them on your device, or turn on iCloud Drive to sync across your iPhone, iPad, and Mac • Open and edit the same files in any other app that reads text • Nothing is locked in a proprietary format, and nothing needs this app to survive Accessibility: Developed toward WCAG 2.2 Level AA and tested with VoiceOver as a primary interaction method. • A predictable, linear VoiceOver reading order • Native controls with the roles and behaviors you already expect • Dynamic Type, including accessibility text sizes, everywhere • System, monospaced, rounded, and serif editor typefaces • Light, dark, and system appearance • Voice Control, Switch Control, and hardware keyboard support • Optional keyboard shortcuts for common actions • Reduced-motion support Privacy: No accounts. No sign-in. No ads. No analytics. No tracking. No data collection of any kind. There is no server behind this app because there doesn't need to be one. Your documents are yours, on your device or in your own iCloud, and they never travel anywhere you don't send them. Made by a blind developer who got tired of using tools that treated screen reader support as an afterthought. Heading

news.title: Apple Releases iOS 26.6.2 and iPadOS 26.6.2 with Fix for Problems Downloading Updates over Cellular Connections
news.summary: Apple has today released iOS 26.6.2 and iPadOS 26.6.2, bringing a fix for an issue that prevented users from downloading updates over cellular connections. As iOS 26.6.2 and iPadOS 26.6.2 were not distributed to external testers prior to their release, we do not have any information on whether they contain any accessibility fixes for blind, deaf blind, or low vision users at the time of writing. However, as these updates appear to have been released to address a specific issue, we do not expect them to contain any such fixes. Release Notes iOS 26.6.2 This update fixes an issue that prevents downloading a software update over a cellular connection. iPadOS 26.6.2 This update fixes an issue that prevents downloading a software update over a cellular connection. How to Update iOS and iPadOS 26.6.2 are available via Over-the-Air Update (Settings > General > Software Update), via Finder on a Mac with macOS Catalina or later, or via iTunes on a PC or Mac with macOS Mojave or earlier. Before updating, we strongly recommend making a full and complete backup of your device (either locally or in iCloud, depending on personal preference). This will ensure that, in the unlikely event that something goes wrong during the update process, you will have a current backup on hand in case a device restore becomes necessary. Also, if using OTA update, we recommend plugging your device into a power source for the duration of the download/installation process, so as to prevent the unlikely event of your battery going dead during the update.

news.title: Apple Introduces Updated Mac Mini and Mac Studio with Upgraded Chips and Improved Connectivity
news.summary: Apple today updated the Mac mini and Mac Studio, introducing the M6 Chip for the Mac mini, as well as the M5 Ultra Chip for the Mac Studio, which Apple describes as its "most powerful silicon ever." Mac mini The new Mac mini with M6 delivers up to 4x faster AI performance, up to 2x faster graphics and storage, and Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and 2.5 gigabit Ethernet connectivity, according to Apple's press release for the Mac Mini . Apple lists the following additional claims related to the Mac Mini with M6: Up to 13.5x faster LLM prompt processing in LM Studio when compared to Mac mini with M1, and up to 4.8x faster than M4. Up to 2.3x faster spreadsheet calculations in Microsoft Excel when compared to Mac mini with M1, and up to 1.5x faster than M4. Up to 2x faster gaming performance with ray tracing in Cyberpunk 2077: Ultimate Edition when compared to Mac mini with M4. In addition to the M6, the Mac mini is also available with M5 Pro, which Apple claims delivers: Up to 8.5x faster LLM prompt processing performance in LM Studio when compared to Mac mini with M2 Pro, and up to 4x faster than M4 Pro. Up to 4.5x faster rendering performance with ray tracing in Blender when compared to Mac mini with M2 Pro, and up to 1.4x faster than M4 Pro. Up to 2.1x faster image processing in Affinity when compared to Mac mini with M2 Pro, and up to 1.5x faster than M4 Pro. Besides the upgraded chips, the new Mac mini features Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, and 2.5GB Ethernet by default (up from the prior generation's default 1GB Ethernet port), with a 10GB option available. The new Mac mini can be preordered from Apple today for a starting price of US $899, and will begin shipping on Tuesday, September 22. Mac Studio Apple has also updated the Mac Studio, bringing the M5 Max and new M5 Ultra chip to Apple's most high-end Mac, as well as Thunderbolt 5, Wi-Fi 7, and Bluetooth 6 connectivity, and a "next-generation SSD architecture that is up to twice as fast as before," according to Apple's press release for the Mac Studio The new Mac Studio with M5 Max delivers up to 3.9x faster AI performance than the prior generation, with the M5 Ultra delivering up to 4.3x the peak AI performance of the M3 Ultra, and up to 9.8x the peak AI performance of the M1 Ultra. Apple additionally lists the following claims related to Mac Studio with M5 Max: Up to 10.7x faster LLM prompt processing in LM Studio when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Max, and 3.9x faster than M4 Max. Up to 7.4x faster text-to-image performance when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Max, and up to 3.5x faster than M4 Max. Up to 5.3x faster Magic Mask performance in Blackmagic Design DaVinci Resolve Studio when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Max, and up to 3x faster than M4 Max. Up to 3.5x faster basecalling for DNA sequencing in Oxford Nanopore MinKNOW when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Max, and up to 1.9x faster than M4 Max. In addition to the M5 Max, the new Mac Studio is available with the new M5 Ultra, which Apple claims delivers: Up to 15.4x faster CopyCat ML training performance in Foundry Nuke when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Ultra, and up to 3.3x faster than M3 Ultra. Up to 9.8x faster LLM prompt processing in LM Studio when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Ultra, and up to 4x faster than M3 Ultra. Up to 8.2x faster text-to-image performance when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Ultra, and up to 4.3x faster than M3 Ultra. Up to 4.7x faster scene rendering performance in Maxon Redshift when compared to Mac Studio with M1 Ultra, and up to 1.7x faster than M3 Ultra. In addition, the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra is available with up to 512 GB of unified memory with 1.2TB/S of memory bandwidth, 50% higher memory bandwidth than M3 Ultra. The new Mac Studio can be preordered from Apple today for a starting price of US $2,499, and most models will begin shipping on Tuesday, September 22, with the model with 512GB of memory shipping in late October.
